column2: This portion of the sixth section is the one from which the sea has withdrawn, among the middle sections of this zone. After it a little of the ninth section is uncovered, and more of the tenth, in which are the upper parts of the lands of China; among its famous cities is Khānkū, and opposite it, to the east, are the islands of al-Sīlān, which have already been mentioned. This is the end of the discussion of the first zone. God, glory be to Him, the Exalted, is the guardian of success, by His grace and bounty.
The second zone:

It adjoins the first on the north. Opposite its west, in the Encircling Ocean, are two of the Fortunate Islands, which were mentioned before. In the first and second sections of it, on the upper side of them, is the land of Qanūriya, and after it, to the east, the upper parts of the land of Ghāna, then the roaming grounds of the Zaghāwa of the Sudan. On the lower side of them is the desert of Nastar, extending from west to east, a land of wastes through which the merchants travel between the lands of the Maghrib and the lands of the Sudan. In it are the roaming grounds of the Veiled People (al-Mulaththamūn) of Ṣanhāja, who are many peoples, among them Kazūla, Lamtūna, Masrāta, Lamṭa and Warīka. In line with these wastes to the east is the land of Fazzān, then the roaming grounds of the Azkār, of the Berber tribes, extending to the upper part of the third section, in line with it to the east. After it, in this third section, on its northern side, is the rest of the land of Waddān, and in line with it to the east the land of Santariyya, which is called the Inner Oases. In the fourth section, in its upper part, is the rest of the land of the Bujā. Then across the middle of this section runs the land of Upper Egypt, the banks of the Nile, which goes from its beginning in the first zone to its mouth in the sea. In this section it passes between the two mountains that enclose it, the Mountain of the Oases on its west and Mount Muqaṭṭam on its east, and on it, in its upper part, are the town of Isnā and Armant

and its banks continue likewise to Asyūṭ and Qūṣ, then to Ṣūl, where the Nile divides into two branches, of which the right ends in this section at al-Lāhūn and the left at Dalāṣ; between them are the upper parts of the lands of Egypt. In the east of Mount Muqaṭṭam are the deserts of ʿAydhāb, running on in the fifth section until they end at the Sea of Suez, which is the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea), descending from the Indian Ocean in the south toward the north. On its eastern shore in this section is the land of the Hijaz, from Mount Yalamlam to the land of Yathrib (Medina); in the middle of the Hijaz is Mecca, may God ennoble it, and on its coast the city of Jidda, which faces the town of ʿAydhāb on the western shore of this sea.

In the sixth section, on its west, is the land of Najd, its upper part in the south, and Tabāla and Jurash up to ʿUkāẓ in the north. Below Najd in this section is the rest of the land of the Hijaz, and in line with it to the east are the lands of Najrān and Khaybar, and below them the land of al-Yamāma. In line with Najrān to the east is the land of Sabaʾ and Maʾrib, then the land of al-Shiḥr, which ends at the Persian Gulf, the second sea descending from the Indian Ocean to the north, as already mentioned. It runs in this section veering to the west, and between its east and its north there passes a triangular portion, on which, at its upper part, is the city of Qalhāt, which is the coast of al-Shiḥr, and below it on its coast the land of ʿUmān. Then the land of al-Baḥrayn, of which Hajar is at the end of the section. In the seventh section, in the upper part of its west, a portion of the Persian Gulf joins the other portion in the sixth, and the Indian Ocean floods its whole upper side, and on it there are the lands of Sind as far as the land of Makrān; opposite it is the land of al-Ṭūbarān, which is also part of Sind, so that the whole of Sind is joined on the western side of this section, and wastes lie between it and the land of India. Its river, which comes from the direction of the land of India, runs through it and flows into the Indian Ocean in the south. The first of the lands of India is on the coast of the Indian Ocean, and in line with it to the east is the land of Balhara, and below it al-Multān, the land of the idol that they hold in great reverence, then down to below Sind, then to the upper parts of the land of Sijistān.

In the eighth section, on its west, is the rest of the land of Balhara of India, and in line with it to the east the land of Qandahār, then the land of Munībār on the upper side, on the coast of the Indian Ocean, and below it on the lower side the land of Kābul, and after it to the east, as far as the Encircling Ocean, the land of Qanawj, between Inner Qashmīr and Outer Qashmīr, at the end of the zone. In the ninth section, then on its western side, is the land of Far India, which continues in it to the eastern side, so that it joins from its upper part to the tenth; and at the bottom of that side there remains a portion of the land of China, in which is the city of Shayghūn; then the land of China joins on through the whole of the tenth section to the Encircling Ocean. God and His Messenger know best, and success is through Him, glory be to Him; He is the guardian of bounty and generosity.
The third zone:

It adjoins the second on the north. In its first section, at about a third from its upper side, Mount Daren cuts across it, from its west at the Encircling Ocean to the east at its end. Nations of Berbers live on this mountain whom none can count but their Creator, as will be mentioned. In the portion between this mountain and the second zone, on the Encircling Ocean, is the ribāṭ of Māssa; joined to it on the east are the lands of Sūs and Nūl, and in line with them to the east the land of Darʿa, then the land of Sijilmāsa, then a portion of the desert of Nastar, the wasteland we mentioned in the second zone. This mountain overlooks all these lands in this section, and it has few passes and routes in this western part until it comes level with the Wādī Mulūya, where its passes and routes become many, until it ends. In this part of it are the nations of the Maṣāmida, then Hintāta, then Tīn Mallal, then Kadmīwa, then Mashkūra, who are the last of the Maṣāmida in it; then the tribes of Ṣanhāka, who are the Ṣanhāja. At the end of this section of it are some of the tribes of Zanāta, and joined to it there, on its north, is Mount Awrās, which is the mountain of the Kutāma; and after that other nations of the Berbers, whom we shall mention in their places.

Now this Mount Daren, on its western side, overlooks the lands of the Far Maghrib, which lie to its north. In the southern region of them are the lands of Marrakesh, Aghmāt and Tādlā, and on the Encircling Ocean from them the ribāṭ of Asfī and the city of Salé. To the north of the land of Marrakesh are the lands of Fez, Meknes, Taza and Qaṣr Kutāma. These are what is called the Far Maghrib in the usage of its inhabitants, and on the coast of the Encircling Ocean from it are the towns of Aṣīlā and al-ʿArāʾish. In line with these lands to the east is the land of the Middle Maghrib, whose capital is Tlemcen; on its coasts, on the Mediterranean, are the towns of Hunayn, Oran and Algiers. For this Mediterranean issues from the Encircling Ocean at the Gulf of Tangier, in the western region of the fourth zone, and goes eastward until it ends at the land of Syria. When it has left the narrow gulf, not far off, it widens to the south and to the north and enters the third zone and the fifth; for this reason many of the lands of this third zone lie on its coast. Then, adjoining the land of Algiers on its east, is the land of Bijāya on the sea coast, then Constantine to the east of it, at the end of the first section and a stage from this sea, in the south of these lands

and, going up to the south of the Middle Maghrib, the town of Ashīr, then the town of al-Masīla, then the Zāb, whose capital is Biskra, below Mount Awrās, which is joined to Daren, as mentioned; this is at the end of this section on the east side. The second section of this zone is of the same form as the first: Mount Daren runs through it at about a third from its south, going through it from west to east and dividing it into two portions, and the Mediterranean floods a stretch of its north. In the southern portion, south of Mount Daren, all of the west is wastes, and in the east of it is the town of Ghadāmis, and in line with it to the east the land of Waddān, the rest of which is in the second zone, as mentioned. The northern portion, north of Mount Daren, between it and the Mediterranean, has in its west Mount Awrās, Tabassa and al-Awbas, and on the sea coast the town of Būna. Then in line with these lands to the east is the land of Ifrīqiya: on the sea coast the city of Tunis, then Sousse, then Mahdia. In the south of these lands, below Mount Daren, are the lands of al-Jarīd, Tozeur, Gafsa and Nafzāwa, and between it and the coasts the city of Qayrawān, Mount Waslāt and Sbeitla. In line with all these lands to the east is the town of Tripoli on the Mediterranean, and facing it in the south Mount Dammar and Naqra, of the tribes of Hawwāra, joined to Mount Daren

and opposite Ghadāmis, which was mentioned at the end of the southern portion, and at the end of this section in the east, is Suwayqat Ibn Mashkūra on the sea, and to the south of it are the roaming grounds of the Arabs in the land of Waddān. In the third section of this zone Mount Daren also runs, except that at its end it bends to the north and goes on in line with it until it enters the Mediterranean, where it is called the Cape of Awthān; and the Mediterranean from the north floods a part of it until it narrows the space between it and Mount Daren. What is behind the mountain, in the south and in the west of it, is the rest of the land of Waddān and the roaming grounds of the Arabs in it, then Zawīla of Ibn Khaṭṭāb, then sands and wastelands to the end of the section in the east. Between the mountain and the sea, in the west of it, is the town of Surt on the sea, then empty tracts and wastelands where the Arabs roam, then Ajdābiya, then Barqa at the bend of the mountain, then Ṭalmasa on the sea there; then in the east of the bend of the mountain are the roaming grounds of Hayb and Rawāḥa to the end of the section. In the fourth section of this zone, in the upper part of its west, are the deserts of Barqīq, and below them the land of Hayb and Rawāḥa; then the Mediterranean enters this section and floods a part of it to the south until it crowds its upper end

and there remain between it and the end of the section wastelands in which the Arabs roam, and in line with them to the east is the land of al-Fayyūm, which lies at the mouth of one of the two branches of the Nile, the one that passes al-Lāhūn in Upper Egypt, in the fourth section of the second zone, and flows into the lake of Fayyūm. In line with it to the east is the land of Egypt and its famous city, on the second branch, which passes Dalāṣ in Upper Egypt at the end of the second section. This branch divides a second time, from below Miṣr, into two other branches, from Shaṭanūf and Zifta, and the right-hand one of them divides at Qarmaṭ into two other branches, and all of them flow into the Mediterranean. On the mouth of the western of these branches is the town of Alexandria, on the mouth of the middle one the town of Rashīd (Rosetta), and on the mouth of the eastern one the town of Damietta. Between Miṣr and Cairo and these sea coasts, the lower parts of the lands of Egypt are all filled with settlement and cultivated land. In the fifth section of this zone are the lands of Syria, most of them, as I shall describe. This is because the Sea of Qulzum ends from the south, and in the west of it, at Suez; for in its course, beginning from the Indian Ocean toward the north, it bends, turning to the west, so that a portion of its bend lies long in the section, and it ends at its western extremity at Suez. And on this portion, after Suez,

are Fārān, then Mount al-Ṭūr, then Ayla of Madyan, then al-Ḥawrāʾ at the end of it; and from there it bends along its coast to the south in the land of the Hijaz, as mentioned in the second zone, in the fifth section of it. In the northern part of this section is a portion of the Mediterranean that has flooded much of its west, on which are al-Farmā and al-ʿArīsh; its end comes close to the town of al-Qulzum, narrowing what is between them there, and something like a door remains, leading into the land of Syria. West of this door is the plain of the Wandering, a barren land where nothing grows, which was the roaming ground of the Children of Israel for forty years after they left Egypt and before they entered Syria, as the Qurʾān recounts. In this portion of the Mediterranean in this section is a part of the island of Cyprus, the rest of it being in the fourth zone, as we shall mention. On the coast of this portion, at the narrowed end of the Sea of Suez, are the town of al-ʿArīsh, which is the last of the lands of Egypt, and Ascalon, and between them is the end of this sea. Then this portion descends, in its bend from there, into the fourth zone at Tripoli and Gaza, and there the Mediterranean ends in the east; and on this portion are most of the coasts of Syria: in the east of it Gaza, then Ascalon

and, deviating slightly from it to the north, the town of Caesarea, and likewise the town of Acre, then Tyre, then Sidon; then the sea bends to the north in the fourth zone. Facing these coastal towns of this portion, in this section, is a great mountain that comes out of the coast of Ayla on the Sea of Qulzum and runs in the northern direction, veering to the east, until it passes beyond this section; it is called Mount Lukkām, and it is as if it were a barrier between the land of Egypt and Syria. At its end, at Ayla, is al-ʿAqaba, over which the pilgrims pass from Egypt to Mecca; then beyond it, in the northern direction, is the burial place of al-Khalīl [Abraham], blessings and peace be upon him, by Mount al-Sarāt, which joins from the aforementioned Mount Lukkām, from the north of al-ʿAqaba, going in line with the east, then bends slightly. In the east of it there are the town of al-Ḥijr, the abodes of Thamūd, Taymāʾ and Dūmat al-Jandal, which are the lower parts of the Hijaz; above them are Mount Raḍwā and the fortresses of Khaybar, to the south of them; and between Mount al-Sarāt and the Sea of Qulzum is the desert of Tabūk. North of Mount al-Sarāt is the city of Jerusalem, at Mount Lukkām, then al-Urdunn, then Tiberias; and east of them the land of al-Ghawr as far as Adhriʿāt, and in line with it Dūmat al-Jandal, the end of this section, which is the end of the Hijaz.

At the bend of Mount Lukkām to the north, at the end of this section, is the city of Damascus, facing Sidon and Beirut of the sea portion, with Mount Lukkām cutting across between it and them. In line with Damascus to the east is the city of Baalbek, then the city of Homs in the northern direction, at the end of the section, where Mount Lukkām breaks off. East of Baalbek and Homs are the town of Tadmur and the roaming grounds of the desert to the end of the section. In the sixth section, in its upper part, are the roaming grounds of the Bedouin Arabs, below the lands of Najd and al-Yamāma, between Mount al-ʿArj and al-Ṣimmān, as far as al-Baḥrayn and Hajar on the Persian Gulf. In the lower parts of this section, below the roaming grounds, are the town of al-Ḥīra and al-Qādisiyya and the marshes of the Euphrates. And after them to the east is the city of Basra. In this section the Persian Gulf ends, at ʿAbbādān and al-Ubulla, in the lower parts of the section, in its north, and into it at ʿAbbādān flows the river Tigris, after dividing into many channels, with other channels of the Euphrates mingling with it; then all of them join at ʿAbbādān and flow into the Persian Gulf. This portion of the sea is wide in its upper part, narrowing at its end in its east, and narrow at its termination, crowding upon its northern boundary. On its western shore are the lower parts of al-Baḥrayn, Hajar and al-Aḥsāʾ, and west of it Akhṭab, al-Ṣimmān and the rest of the land of al-Yamāma, and on its eastern shore the coasts of Fārs, from its upper part

and it lies from the end of the section in the east, on an arm that has extended from this sea eastward, and behind it to the south in this section are the Qufṣ mountains of Kirmān; and below Hormuz, on the coast, the town of Sīrāf, and Najīram on the coast of this sea, and in the east of it to the end of this section. Below Hormuz are the lands of Fārs, such as Sābūr, Dārabjird, Nasā, Iṣṭakhr, al-Shāhjān and Shīrāz, which is the capital of all of them; and below the land of Fārs, to the north, at the end of the sea, are the lands of Khūzistān, among them al-Ahwāz, Tustar, Ṣadā, Sābūr, al-Sūs, Rāmhurmuz and others, and Arrajān, which is the boundary between Fārs and Khūzistān. East of the land of Khūzistān are the mountains of the Kurds, extending to the districts of Isfahan; in them are their dwellings, and their roaming grounds are behind them in the land of Fārs, which is called al-Rusūm. In the seventh section, in the upper part of it in the west, are the rest of the Qufṣ mountains, followed on the south and north by the lands of Kirmān and Makrān; among its cities are al-Rūdhān, al-Shīrajān, Jīraft, Yazdshīr and al-Bahraj; and below the land of Kirmān to the north is the rest of the land of Fārs to the borders of Isfahan, and the city of Isfahan is at the edge of this section between its west and its north. Then, in the east of the lands of Kirmān and Fārs, is the land of Sijistān and Kūhistān in the south, and the land of Kūhistān to the north of it; and between Kirmān and Fārs and between Sijistān and Kūhistān, in the middle of this section, lie the great wastes, with few routes because of their difficulty. Among the cities of Sijistān are Bust and al-Ṭāq. As for Kūhistān, it is one of the lands of Khurāsān, and among its famous towns are Sarakhs and Quhistān, at the end of the section.

In the eighth section, in its west and south, are the roaming grounds of the Khalaj, of the nations of the Turks, adjoining the land of Sijistān on its west and the land of Kābul of India on its south. To the north of these roaming grounds are the mountains of Ghūr and its lands, whose capital is Ghazna, the port of India; at the end of Ghūr in the north is the land of Astarābādh; then in the north, toward the west, to the end of the section, is the land of Herat, the middle of Khurāsān, in which are Asfarāyin, Qāshān, Būshanj, Marw al-Rūdh, al-Ṭāliqān and al-Jūzjān; and Khurāsān there ends at the river Jayḥūn. On this river, of the lands of Khurāsān, on its west is the city of Balkh and on its east the city of Tirmidh; the city of Balkh was the seat of the kingdom of the Turks. This river, the Jayḥūn, has its source in the land of Wajār, in the territory of Badhakhshān, on the side adjoining India, and it comes out from the south of this section and at its end in the east, then bends soon to the west to the middle of the section, where it is called the river of Kharnāb, then bends to the north until it passes through Khurāsān and goes on in that direction until it flows into the lake of Khwārazm in the fifth zone, as we shall mention. And it is fed, at its bend in

the middle of the section, from south to north, by five great rivers from the lands of al-Khuttal and al-Wakhsh, on its east, and by other rivers from the mountains of al-Butm, also on its east, and from the north of the mountain, until it widens and grows great beyond compare. Of these five rivers that feed it is the Wakhshāb, which comes out of the land of Tibet, which lies between the south and the east of this section, and passes westward veering to the north until it comes out into the ninth section near the north of this section; a great mountain crosses its path, which runs from the middle of the south in this section and goes eastward veering to the north until it comes out into the ninth section near the north of this section; it passes the land of Tibet to the south-eastern portion of this section and stands between the Turks and the land of al-Khuttal. It has only one route, in the middle of the east of this section, in which al-Faḍl ibn Yaḥyā made a barrier and built a gate like the Barrier of Gog and Magog. When the river Wakhshāb comes out of the land of Tibet and this mountain crosses its path, it passes beneath it for a long stretch until it passes through the land of al-Wakhsh

and flows into the Jayḥūn at the borders of Balkh, then it passes it slowly to Tirmidh in the north, to the land of al-Jūzjān. East of the land of Ghūr, between it and the Jayḥūn, is the land of al-Nāsān of Khurāsān; and on the eastern bank there of the river are the land of al-Khuttal, most of which is mountains, and the land of al-Wakhsh, bounded on the north by the mountains of al-Butm, which come out from the edge of Khurāsān, west of the Jayḥūn, and go eastward until their end joins the great mountain behind which lies the land of Tibet and beneath which the Wakhshāb passes, as we have said; so they meet at the gate of al-Faḍl ibn Yaḥyā. The Jayḥūn passes between these mountains, and other rivers flow into it, among them the river of the land of al-Wakhsh, which flows into it from the east, below Tirmidh toward the north; and the river of Balkh, which comes out of the mountains of al-Butm, its beginning at al-Jūzjān, and flows into it from its west. On this river, on its west, is the land of Āmul of Khurāsān, and east of the river there are the land of Sughd, Asr and Shanna, of the lands of the Turks, and east of them the land of Farghāna also, to the end of the section in the east. All the lands of the Turks are enclosed by the mountains of al-Butm to the north of them. In the ninth section, from its west, is the land of Tibet to the middle of the section, and south of it the land of India, and east of it the land of China to the end of the section

and in the lower part of this section, north of the land of Tibet, is the land of the Khazlajiyya, of the lands of the Turks, to the end of the section in the east and north; adjoining it on its west is the land of Farghāna also, to the end of the section in the east; and on its east is the land of the Ṭughurghur, of the Turks, to [the end of] the section in the east and north. In the tenth section, in the south of it entirely, is the rest of China and its lower parts, and in the north the rest of the land of the Ṭughurghur; then east of them the land of Khirkhīr, of the Turks also, to the end of the section in the east; and in the north of the land of Khirkhīr the land of Kitmān, of the Turks. Opposite it in the Encircling Ocean is the island of Rubies, in the middle of a circular mountain, with no passage or route into it, and climbing to the top of it from outside is extremely hard; in the island are deadly snakes and many pebbles of ruby, so the people of that region find ways, as God inspires them. The people of these lands in this ninth and tenth section, beyond Khurāsān and the mountains, are all roaming grounds of the Turks, countless nations, and they are migrants and wanderers, people of camels, sheep, cattle and horses, kept for breeding, riding and eating. Their groups are many, and none can count them but their Creator. Among them are Muslims, on the side adjoining the lands of the River, the river Jayḥūn, and they raid the unbelievers among them who follow Magianism and sell their slaves to those next to them, and they go out to the lands of Khurāsān, India and Iraq
The fourth zone:

It adjoins the third on the north. The first section of it has in its west a portion of the Encircling Ocean, elongated from its beginning in the south to its end in the north, and on it in the south is the city of Tangier. From this portion, below Tangier, the Mediterranean issues from the Encircling Ocean, in a narrow gulf of about twelve miles, between Tarifa and Algeciras in the north and Qaṣr al-Majāz and Ceuta in the south, and it goes eastward until it ends in the middle of the fifth section of this zone, widening gradually as it goes until it floods the four sections and most of the fifth of this zone, [and parts of] the third and fifth zones, as we shall mention. This sea is also called the Syrian Sea, and in it are many islands, the greatest of them in the west being Ibiza, then Majorca, then Minorca, then Sardinia, then Sicily, which is the greatest of them, then Balūnis, then Crete, then Cyprus, all of which we shall mention in their sections in which they lie. And from this Mediterranean, at the end of the third section of it and in the third section of the fifth zone, issues the Gulf of the Venetians, which goes toward the north, then bends at the middle of the section from its north and passes westward until it ends in the second section of the fifth

and from it too, at the end of the fourth section, in the east, of the fifth zone, issues the Gulf of Constantinople, which passes in the north narrowed to the breadth of an arrow’s shot, to the end of the zone, then leads out into the fourth section of the sixth zone and turns to the Sea of Nīṭish (the Black Sea), going eastward through the whole of the fifth section and half of the sixth of the sixth zone, as we shall mention in their places. When this Mediterranean issues from the Encircling Ocean in the Gulf of Tangier and widens into the third zone, there remains in the south of the gulf a small portion of this section, in which is the city of Tangier at the meeting of the two seas, and after it the city of Ceuta on the Mediterranean, then Qaṭāwun, then Bādīs; then this sea floods the rest of this section in the east and goes out to the third. Most of the settlement in this section is in its north and in the north of the gulf of it, and all of it is the lands of western al-Andalus, those between the Encircling Ocean and the Mediterranean; the first of them is Tarifa at the meeting of the two seas, and east of it on the coast of the Mediterranean Algeciras, then Malaga, then al-Munakkab, then Almeria; and below these, from the Encircling Ocean in the west

and near it, Jerez, then Niebla, and opposite it in it the island of Cadiz; and east of Jerez and Niebla, Seville, then Ecija, Cordoba and Madīla, then Granada, Jaen and Ubeda, then Wādiyāsh and Baza; and below these Shant Mariya and Shilb on the Encircling Ocean in the west; and east of them Badajoz, Merida and Yābura, then Ghāfiq and Bazjāla, then Qalʿat Riyāḥ; and below these Lisbon, on the Encircling Ocean in the west and on the river of Bāja, and east of it Santarem and Mūziya on the aforementioned river, then Qanṭarat al-Sayf. In line with Lisbon on the east is Mount al-Shārāt, which begins in the west there and goes eastward along the end of the section from its north and ends at the city of Sālim, after the middle of it. Below this mountain are Talavera, in the east of Fūrna, then Toledo, then Wādī al-Ḥijāra, then the city of Sālim. At the beginning of this mountain, between it and Lisbon, is the town of Coimbra. This is western al-Andalus.

As for eastern al-Andalus, on its coast of the Mediterranean, after Almeria, are Cartagena, then Lafta, then Denia, then Valencia, to Tortosa, the end of the section in the east; and below it, to the north, Lorca and Shaqūra, which border Baza and Qalʿat Riyāḥ of western al-Andalus; then Murcia to the east; then Shāṭiba, below Valencia to the north; then Shuqr; then Tortosa; then Tarragona, the end of the section; then below these, to the north, the land of Manjāla and Rīda, which border Shaqūra and Toledo on the west; then Fraga in the east, below Tortosa and north of it; then in the east of the city of Sālim, Qalʿat Ayyūb, then Saragossa, then Lerida, the end of the section in the east and north. The second section of this zone is entirely covered by water except a portion of its west in the north, in which is the rest of Mount al-Barnāt, the meaning of which is the mountain of the passes and ways; it comes out to it from the end of the first section of the fifth zone, beginning from the extremity where the Encircling Ocean ends at the end of that section in the south and east, and it passes in the south veering to the east and comes out in this fourth zone, deviating from the first section of it into this second section; a portion of it falls in it, whose passes lead to the mainland, and it is called the land of Ghashkūniya, and in it are the city of Kharīda and Qarqashūna

and on the coast of the Mediterranean from this portion are the city of Barcelona, then Narbonne. In this sea, which has flooded the section, are many islands, and many of them are uninhabited because of their smallness. In the west of it is the island of Sardinia, and in the east of it the island of Sicily, wide in its extent, said to have a circumference of 700 miles; it has many cities, among whose famous ones are Syracuse, Palermo, Ṭarābgha, Māzar and Messina. This island faces the land of Ifrīqiya, and between them are the islands of Aʿdūsh and Malta. The third section of this zone is also covered by the sea except for three portions on the north side: the western of them is the land of Qalūriya, the middle one is of the land of Abkīrda, and the eastern one is of the lands of the Venetians.

The fourth section of this zone is also covered by the sea, as mentioned, and its islands are many, most of them uninhabited as in the third; the inhabited among them are the island of Balūnis in the north-western part and the island of Crete, elongated from the middle of the section to between the south and the east of it. The fifth section of this zone: the sea has flooded from it a large triangle between the south and the west, the western side of which ends at the end of the section in the north and its southern side ends at about two thirds of the section; and there remains on the eastern side of the section a portion of about a third, the northern part of which passes to the west, bending along with the sea, as we said, and in the southern half of it are the lower parts of Syria. Through the middle of it runs Mount Lukkām until it ends at the end of Syria in the north, and there it bends, going toward the north-eastern quarter, and after its bend it is called the Chain Mountain; and from there it goes out into the fifth zone

and from its bend it passes a portion of the lands of al-Jazīra to the east, and from its bend on the west rise mountains joined one to another until it ends at an arm that projects from the Mediterranean, set back to the end of the section in the north; between these mountains are passes called al-Durūb, which lead out to the land of the Armenians; and in this section is a portion of them, between these mountains and the Chain Mountain. As for the southern side, where we said are the lower parts of Syria and that Mount Lukkām cuts across it between the Mediterranean and the end of the section from south to north: on the sea coast is the town of Anṭarṭūs at the beginning of the section in the south, adjoining Gaza and Tripoli on its coast, in the third zone; and north of Anṭarṭūs are Jabala, then Latakia, then Iskandarūna, then Salūqiya, and after it in the north the lands of the Rūm. As for Mount Lukkām, cutting across between the sea and the end of the section along its flanks, there adjoins it, of the lands of Syria, in the upper part of the section, in the south, on its west, the fortress of al-Ḥawānī, which belongs to the Ismāʿīlī Ḥashīshiyya, who in this age are known as the Fidāwiyya, and it is called Maṣyāt, and it is opposite Anṭarṭūs; and opposite this fortress, east of the mountain, is the town of Salamiyya, north of Homs; and in the north, in Maṣyāt, between the mountain and the sea, is the town of Antioch

and opposite it, east of the mountain, al-Maʿarra, and east of it al-Marāgha; and north of Antioch al-Maṣṣīṣa, then Adhana, then Tarsus, the end of Syria; and level with it, west of the mountain, Qinnasrīn, then ʿAyn Zarba; and opposite Qinnasrīn, east of the mountain, Aleppo; and opposite ʿAyn Zarba, Manbij, the end of Syria. As for al-Durūb, on their right, between them and the Mediterranean, is the land of the Rūm, which at this time belongs to the Turkmen, and its sultan is Ibn ʿUthmān; on the sea coast of it are the towns of Antalya and al-ʿAlāyā. As for the land of the Armenians that is between the mountain of al-Durūb and the Chain Mountain, in it are the town of Marʿash, Malaṭya and al-Maʿarra, to the end of the northern section. And there come out of the fifth section, in the land of the Armenians, the river Jayḥān and, east of it, the river Sayḥān; the Jayḥān passes through it southward until it passes beyond al-Durūb, then passes Tarsus, then al-Maṣṣīṣa, then bends, descending to the north and west, until it flows into the Mediterranean south of Salūqiya; the river Sayḥān runs parallel to the river Jayḥān and goes alongside al-Maʿarra and Marʿash and passes beyond the mountains of al-Durūb into the land of Syria; then it passes ʿAyn Zarba and departs from the river Jayḥān; then it bends to the north, westward, and mingles with the river Jayḥān at al-Maṣṣīṣa

and from its west. As for the land of al-Jazīra, which is encircled by the bend of Mount Lukkām to the Chain Mountain, in its south are al-Rāfiqa and al-Raqqa, then Ḥarrān, then Sarūj and al-Ruhā, then Naṣībīn, then Sumaysāṭ and Āmid, below the Chain Mountain and the end of the section on its north, which is also the end of the section on its east. Through the middle of this portion run the Euphrates and the Tigris; they come out of the fifth zone and pass through the land of the Armenians southward until they pass beyond the Chain Mountain. The Euphrates passes west of Sumaysāṭ and Sarūj, veers to the east, passes near al-Rāfiqa and al-Raqqa, and goes out into the sixth section; the Tigris passes east of Āmid, bends to the east nearby, and goes out shortly into the sixth section. In the sixth section of this zone, on its west, is the land of al-Jazīra, and east of it the land of Iraq, joined to it, ending in the east near the end of the section; and across the end of Iraq there runs the mountain of Isfahan, descending from the south of the section veering to the west; when it reaches the middle of the section from its end in the north, it goes westward until it leaves the sixth section and joins, in its line, the Chain Mountain in the fifth section. So this sixth section is cut into two portions, western and eastern. In the western, in the south of it, is the exit of the Euphrates from the fifth

and in the north of it the exit of the Tigris from it. As for the Euphrates, as soon as it comes out into the sixth it passes Qarqīsiyāʾ, and a channel goes out from there to the north, flowing through the land of al-Jazīra and sinking into its districts; it passes on from Qarqīsiyā not far, then bends to the south and passes near the Khābūr, to the west of al-Raḥba, and channels go out from it there; it passes southward, and Ṣiffīn remains on its west, then it bends to the east and divides into branches, some of which pass by Kufa and some by Qaṣr Ibn Hubayra and al-Jāmiʿayn, and all of them go out in the south of the section into the third zone and sink there, in the east of al-Ḥīra and al-Qādisiyya. And the Euphrates goes out from al-Raḥba eastward in its line to Hīt, from its north, passes to al-Zāb and al-Anbār from their south, and then flows into the Tigris at Baghdad. As for the river Tigris, when it enters this section from the fifth it passes Jazīrat Ibn ʿUmar on its north, then Mosul likewise, and Tikrīt, and reaches al-Ḥadītha, where it bends to the south, and al-Ḥadītha remains on its east, and the Greater and Lesser Zāb likewise; it goes on in its line southward and to the west of al-Qādisiyya until it reaches Baghdad and mingles with the Euphrates; then it passes southward to the west of Jarjarāyā until it leaves the section into the third zone, and there its branches and channels spread out, then gather and flow into the Persian Gulf there, at ʿAbbādān. And what lies between the river Tigris and the Euphrates, before their meeting at Baghdad, is the land of al-Jazīra

and there mingles with the river Tigris, after it leaves Baghdad, another river that comes from its north-eastern direction and ends at the land of al-Nahrawān, opposite Baghdad to the east, then bends to the south and mingles with the Tigris before it goes out into the third zone; and between this river and the mountain of Iraq and the non-Arabs there remain the town of Jalūlāʾ and, in the east of it, at the mountain, the towns of Ḥulwān and Ṣaymara.
